doc.title: Bill Goodwin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 28, 2025

chapter: Coming up on the L.A. scene
title: Ornette Coleman, Contemporary Records and playing with Peacock, Budimir and Shank
summary: What 'adventurous' meant on the west coast: love of Ornette and Contemporary Records, and playing with Gary Peacock, Dennis Budimir and Bud Shank at Shelly's Manne-Hole.

story.theme_name: Playing with Coltrane and the avant-garde

blocks.x: Can you define “adventurous” at that point in the west coast jazz scene?

Ornette Coleman’s first record came out, the second record came out while I was still in high school, and I loved them, I bought them and I loved them. The reason I bought them was they were on Contemporary Records which was my favorite label, and I had already got to meet and, you know as a teenager gotten to meet and play with Art Pepper and I listened to “Shelly Manne and His Men” were on that label and I loved everything on Contemporary Records. I would just get it, and I saw Ornette Coleman on the album with his plastic saxophone and said, “Who’s this guy?” You know, had to check it out, and I just fell in love with his music. And so that was where Gary was in that camp, and we played a lot with Dennis Budimir, he’s a great guitarist and we often worked with Bud Shank who had a regular night at Shelly’s Manne-Hole, like an off night, a weeknight.
Now those guys followed the path into the studios and I’m assuming they made a pretty good living. Did you aspire to that?
